newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sees less impact of hog disease on jobless.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sees less impact of hog disease on jobless.

text.p: Taiwan's jobless rate slipped in March, official data on Wednesday showed, forcing economists to scale back their projections of how many jobs would be lost following an outbreak of hog disease last month.
Taiwan's unemployment rate slipped to 2.79 percent in March from 2.97 percent in February, the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics said on Wednesday.
Officials and economists said the hog disease will push up Taiwan's jobless rate in April but the impact may not be as big as originally expected. The April jobless rate will be released in late May.
Officials and economists had predicted in March that the outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease on March 20 would raise the island's jobless rate in each subsequent month to reach around 3.0 percent.
Before the outbreak, the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development had set a jobless target of 2.6 percent for 1997.

Following Wednesday's announcement of a lower-than-expected jobless rate in March, analysts said the hog disease epidemic, despite cutting off Taiwan's pork export sector, would not trigger soaring unemployment.

"The hog epidemic still will worsen the jobless problem, but it seems that my original estimate that it would add 0.5 percentage points to April's jobless rate is too high," said Core Pacific economist J.C. Yang.
"I would add only 0.1 percentage point on it now."

Economists said increasing employment possibilities existed, noting the government's announcement on Tuesday of higher-than-expected March export orders and industrial output growth, which could compensate for the loss of jobs caused by the epidemic.
Taiwan's March export orders rose 5.61 percent year-on-year and industrial output increased 10.01 percent.
"Domestic demand keeps on rising, and it should gradually improve unemployment," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
"Many new construction projects had been launched since late March on anticipation of a recovering property market, and this should help reduce joblessness," Huang said.
Both Huang and Core Pacific's Yang said the jobless rate for the whole of 1997 would hover around 2.6-2.7 percent.
The directorate had said that about 100,000 people may lose their jobs due to the hog disease epidemic.
Taiwan lifted the export ban on April 17, but major importing countries, including Japan and South Korea, have maintained their ban on Taiwan pork.
Cheng Shuo-liang, a directorate section-chief, told reporters on Wednesday he expected the jobless rate to climb in April due to the epidemic.
"The hog disease's impact on jobless rate will start to show in April," Cheng said. "But we cannot predict how serious it will be and how long it will last."
But economists said a government-backed campaign to promote local pork sales would lessen the impact of the outbreak.
Taiwan's jobless rate hovered close to 1.5 percent from 1991-1994, rose to 1.79 percent in 1995 and pushed above 3.0 percent from August to October of 1996 before coming back down.
The jobless rate was 2.60 percent for all of 1996, a 10-year high.
